13 A uniform rod of weight 28 N is supported at one end by force F.
The rod is in equilibrium and attached to a frictionless hinge at end X.
F
rod
40°
X
28 N
What is the magnitude of F ?
A
9.0 N
B
11 N
C
18 N
D
21 N

hints: Notice from the right-angle mark that $F$ acts perpendicular to the rod at distance $L$ from hinge X, so its moment about X is $F \times L$.
The uniform $28 \text{ N}$ rod acts vertically at its midpoint, a distance $L/2$ along the rod from X, and the rod makes $40^{\circ}$ with the horizontal.
Take moments about X to eliminate the hinge force, using the horizontal distance $(L/2)\cos 40^{\circ}$ as the perpendicular distance for the vertical weight.
walkthrough: Take moments about hinge X because the unknown hinge force then has zero moment. Let rod length be $L$.
Force $F$ is perpendicular to the rod at the far end, so its anticlockwise moment about X is $F \times L$.
The $28 \text{ N}$ weight acts vertically downwards at the centre, $L/2$ from X along the $40^{\circ}$ rod. Its perpendicular distance from X is the horizontal separation $(L/2)\cos 40^{\circ}$.
Its clockwise moment about X is therefore $28 \times (L/2)\cos 40^{\circ}$.
For equilibrium, sum of moments about X is zero: $F \times L = 28 \times (L/2) \cos 40^{\circ}$.
Cancel $L$ to get $F = 14 \cos 40^{\circ} = 14 \times 0.766 = 10.7 \text{ N}$, about $11 \text{ N}$. This is option B.

A.explanation: This gives $14 \sin 40^{\circ} = 9.0 \text{ N}$. It uses $\sin 40^{\circ}$ instead of $\cos 40^{\circ}$ for the horizontal distance from X to the weight.

B.explanation: Taking moments about X gives $F = 14 \cos 40^{\circ} = 11 \text{ N}$, balancing the moment of the $28 \text{ N}$ weight acting at the midpoint.

C.explanation: This gives $28 \sin 40^{\circ} = 18 \text{ N}$. It uses the wrong angle component and wrongly places the $28 \text{ N}$ weight at the end of the rod.

D.explanation: This gives $28 \cos 40^{\circ} = 21 \text{ N}$. It correctly uses $\cos 40^{\circ}$ but wrongly places the $28 \text{ N}$ weight at the end instead of at $L/2$.
